summary: Describes the reasoning behind a proposed Host Identity namespace and a new protocol layer, the Host Identity Protocol, between the internetworking and transport layers. It covers weaknesses of current namespaces and gives the thinking of the authors as of Fall 2003. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 9063.

eli5.summary: Today a computer's address says where it is. This proposes a separate name that says who it is, so it can move and still be recognized.

questions: what is the host identity protocol
how does hip differ from ip addresses
subtitle: A new namespace between IP addresses and transport to decouple identity from location.

tldr.problem: IP addresses conflate two separate concepts: location (where a host is reachable) and identity (who the host is). This makes mobility, multi-homing, and authentication difficult without changing the transport layer.
tldr.mechanism: The Host Identity Protocol (HIP) introduces a separate Host Identity namespace based on public key cryptography, positioned between the internetworking and transport layers. Transport connections bind to Host Identities rather than IP addresses.
tldr.outcome: Hosts can change IP addresses without breaking connections, support mobility and multi-homing more easily, and authenticate each other cryptographically. This was replaced by RFC 9063.

today: RFC 4423 presents the HIP architecture as of Fall 2003 and is now obsoleted by RFC 9063. HIP has been standardized through the IETF HIP Working Group and IRTF HIP Research Group, and implementations exist, though deployment has been limited. The architecture remains influential in discussions of identity separation and mobility.

sections.title: The Problem with IP Addresses
sections.content:
The Internet has two global namespaces: IP addresses and Domain Name Service (DNS) names. IP addresses encode two pieces of information: the location of a host on the network (routing direction) and the name of a network interface. This semantic overloading is the root of several problems.

When a host moves from one network to another, its IP address changes, breaking transport-layer connections because TCP and UDP identify endpoints by IP address and port. DNS names help for servers but do not solve the problem for general host mobility. A third namespace, based on host identity rather than location, could decouple these concerns and allow transport connections to survive address changes.
sections.eli5: Right now, your computer's IP address is like your home address: it says where you are. If you move, the address changes. This breaks phone calls (TCP connections) because they use your address to find you.

sections.title: Host Identities and Host Identity Tags
sections.content:
A Host Identifier (HI) is a cryptographic public key that uniquely identifies a computing platform. Unlike IP addresses, Host Identifiers are not assigned by infrastructure and do not change when the host relocates. Each host can have multiple identities: some published in DNS (for servers), some unpublished or ephemeral (for clients and anonymous use).

For practical use in protocols, Host Identifiers are hashed into 128-bit Host Identity Tags (HITs). HITs are fixed-length and independent of the cryptographic algorithm used, making them suitable for packet headers and APIs. A Local Scope Identifier (LSI) provides a 32-bit localized representation for compatibility with existing IPv4 protocols and socket APIs.
sections.eli5: Your identity is a secret key you own. To use it in messages, we hash it into a fixed-size number. This number stays the same even if your IP address changes.

sections.title: Separating Identity from Location
sections.content:
In the traditional stack, services bind to IP addresses. A TCP connection from client to server is identified by the tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). If either IP changes, the connection breaks.

HIP introduces a new layer: services and transport associations bind to Host Identities instead. IP addresses remain as locators—information used purely for routing. When a host moves, it updates its locators but keeps its identity constant. Existing transport associations survive. HIP also enables multi-homing: a single host identity can simultaneously be reachable through multiple IP addresses, allowing flexible failover and load balancing.
sections.eli5: Instead of binding to your address, your TCP connection binds to your identity. When you move to a new address, the connection follows you automatically.

sections.title: Mobility and Multi-homing Support
sections.content:
HIP provides two mechanisms for handling address changes. When an address change occurs mid-connection, the mobile node sends a readdress packet to its peer with the new address. However, blindly accepting new addresses would enable distributed denial-of-service attacks: an attacker could open many connections and claim to have moved to a victim's address, flooding it with traffic.

HIP protects against this with a reachability check: before accepting traffic at a new address, the peer verifies that the mobile node is reachable there. For nodes that move infrequently, DNS can publish updated addresses. For truly mobile nodes, a rendezvous mechanism—a static infrastructure service—can store and return the current address of a mobile host based on its HIT.
sections.eli5: When you move, you tell your friends your new address. They check that you are really there before sending lots of data, to stop attackers from tricking them into attacking someone else.

sections.title: Authentication and IPsec Integration
sections.content:
Because Host Identifiers are public keys, they enable cryptographic authentication. HIP defines a HIP base exchange—a four-packet protocol where the responder initiates the authenticated Diffie-Hellman key agreement. This asymmetry protects against denial-of-service attacks by making the responder's initial cost low.

HIP typically works with IPsec (Encapsulating Security Payload in transport mode) to protect the actual data traffic. The Host Identifiers are used to establish IPsec Security Associations (SAs), and the SAs are indexed by the HITs, not the IP addresses. This allows packets to be decrypted and verified even if the source address has changed, as long as the HIT and SPI are correct.
sections.eli5: Your identity proves who you are using math. HIP and IPsec use your identity to set up a secure encrypted tunnel that works even when your address changes.
